titre: A Fossil Reconstructed Upside Down for Fifteen Years
accroche: Described in 1977 as walking on its spines, an animal of the Burgess Shale had to be turned over in 1991. Its real legs were elsewhere.
contenu_vulgarise:
In late August 1909, the American paleontologist Charles Doolittle Walcott, then Secretary of the Smithsonian Institution, is exploring the heights of Mount Field, in British Columbia, when he comes upon an outcrop of black shale riddled with fossils of unusual quality: soft-bodied animals, normally absent from the fossil record, preserved down to the details of their intestines. The deposit, dated to about 508 million years ago, in the middle of the Cambrian, will become the Burgess Shale. Until 1924, Walcott extracts from it more than 65,000 specimens on about 30,000 blocks of rock, but, overwhelmed by his administrative duties, he publishes only preliminary descriptions, and sorts each strange animal into an already known zoological group: jellyfish, shrimp, worm.

## A Reexamination That Changes the Categories

In the 1960s, the British paleontologist Harry Whittington relaunched field campaigns with the Geological Survey of Canada, then reopened the crates of Walcott's specimens, which had remained almost untouched for half a century. With two Cambridge doctoral students, Derek Briggs and Simon Conway Morris, he undertook a complete revision in the 1970s. The finding reverses Walcott's: a good part of this fauna belongs to no animal group known today. These are evolutionary experiments that vanished without descendants, not misidentified cousins of living animals.

## An Animal Named for Its Strangeness, Reconstructed Upside Down

The most spectacular example of this reexamination also illustrates its own limits. In 1977, Conway Morris describes a small animal with a row of rigid spines and a row of soft tentacles, so baffling that he names it *Hallucigenia*. In his reconstruction, the spines serve as legs for walking, and the soft tentacles as arms for feeding. In 1991, the Swedish paleontologist Lars Ramsköld and the Chinese Hou Xianguang describe in *Nature* an armored lobopodian related to *Microdictyon*, found at Chengjiang, an animal different from Hallucigenia, but whose anatomy allows them, by comparison, to propose a complete flip: the rigid spines would not serve for walking, but as dorsal defense; the row of tentacles would in fact be a row of legs. The hypothesis assumes a second, symmetrical row, never observed on a Hallucigenia fossil. Further preparation of these fossils finally reveals it, hidden by lateral crushing: Ramsköld alone publishes the confirmation in 1992, in the journal *Lethaia*.

## What the Complete Story Reveals

None of this discredits the scientific method: it is, on the contrary, its normal workings, in three distinct stages. Walcott forces unprecedented forms into boxes that are too narrow; Whittington and his team open these boxes and reveal an unsuspected diversity, but still get wrong the orientation of one of the strangest animals they describe; Ramsköld, with further preparation of the same fossils, corrects this last error. Each stage rests on more material than the previous one. The correction of a correction is not an admission of failure. It is the normal trace of a science that advances by way of fossils, a century after the first shovelful of black shale.

repere.texte: Walcott extracts more than 65,000 specimens from the Burgess Shale between 1909 and 1924; it would take until the 1970s for a complete revision, led by Whittington, Briggs and Conway Morris, to reveal that a good part of this fauna belongs to no animal group known today.

carte.punch: This fossil was reconstructed upside down between 1977 and 1992.
carte.idee: Described in 1977, Hallucigenia walked, it was believed, on a row of rigid spines. In 1991, another fossil, found in China, suggests turning it over; in 1992, a second row of legs, hidden by the crushing of the fossil, confirms that the spines were dorsal defenses.

quiz.question: Why did the Hallucigenia reconstruction published in 1977 turn out to be upside down?
choix: Because the original fossil had been mislabeled in the museum collections
Because a second row of legs, masked by the crushing of the fossil, was confirmed only in 1992
Because Conway Morris had never examined the fossil in person, only photographs
Because the species had been confused with another from the same fossil deposit
quiz.explication: The original Canadian fossils were crushed laterally, which masked one of the two rows of legs. In 1991, comparison with a related Chinese lobopodian suggests turning the reconstruction over; it is only in 1992, on the Hallucigenia fossils themselves, that Ramsköld confirms this second row.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Who discovers the Burgess Shale deposit, and in what year?
quiz_supplementaire.explication: It is Charles Doolittle Walcott, then Secretary of the Smithsonian Institution, who discovers the deposit in 1909 while exploring Mount Field, in British Columbia.

quiz_supplementaire.question: How did Walcott classify the strange animals he extracted from the Burgess Shale?
choix: He placed them in already known zoological groups, such as jellyfish, shrimp or worm
He considered them all to be species still living elsewhere in the world
He refused to publish them until a classification imposed itself
He created an entirely new phylum for each unusual specimen
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Overwhelmed by his administrative duties, Walcott sorted each strange animal into an already known zoological group, rather than seeing them as extinct forms with no living equivalent.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What allows Ramsköld and Hou to propose, in 1991, turning the Hallucigenia reconstruction over?
choix: A comparison with a living lobopodian found in the Amazon
A new electron microscope examination of the original 1977 fossil
The description of a related armored Chinese lobopodian, found at Chengjiang
The previously unknown testimony of a Walcott assistant found in the archives
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The comparison with this armored Chinese lobopodian, related to Microdictyon but distinct from Hallucigenia, allows Ramsköld and Hou to propose the complete flip of the reconstruction.
